title: The Primary Sector: Agriculture
tagline: Farming as India’s largest employer: types of farming, inputs and outputs, and the sector’s place in the economy.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE Economics syllabus registered in this subject’s baseline (the 2026-27 session syllabus as reproduced by Shaalaa and Jagran Josh; the official cisce.org PDFs were not retrievable). Every question and answer is original practice, no board examination paper was consulted, and no figure is presented as an official statistic.

overview.intro: Agriculture is the oldest and, in India, still the largest economic activity by employment — the primary sector at full scale. This chapter studies it the way the syllabus does: as a system of inputs and outputs, as a classification of farming types, and as a place in the wider economy that supplies food to the population and raw materials to industry. It also treats the pressures the activity works under — land fragmentation, dependence on the monsoon, the gap between yield potential and yield achieved — because understanding agriculture in a developing economy means understanding why a sector that employs so much produces a smaller share of income. The vocabulary of farming, its seasons and its crops, forms the working language of this chapter’s answers.

learningOutcomes: Define agriculture and classify its principal types.
Distinguish subsistence from commercial farming with examples.
List the inputs of farming and the outputs it generates.
Explain the role of agriculture in food supply and industry.
Identify the main challenges facing Indian agriculture.
Explain the government measures that raised agricultural production and assess the Green Revolution’s positive impacts.
Define food security and describe the role of the Food Corporation of India.

learn.title: What agriculture includes, and how it is classified

blocks.text: Agriculture is the cultivation of soil to grow crops and the rearing of animals for food and produce, practised together with forestry and, in common usage, fisheries. Its classification begins with purpose. Subsistence farming grows food mainly to feed the farmer’s own household, with any surplus sold locally — it is small in scale, labour-intensive and risk-exposed. Commercial farming grows crops chiefly for sale, often one or two cash crops, using purchased inputs and market information, and its scale and technique are geared to income rather than to the family’s own consumption. Between these poles lie mixed farms that feed the household first and sell the rest. Other classifications cut differently: by intensity, intensive farming uses much labour and care on small holdings while extensive farming uses much land per worker; by organisation, organised farming is capitalised and market-connected while unorganised farming is small, local and traditional.

blocks.caption: The principal classifications of farming
rows: Subsistence — grows to feed the household
Intensive — much labour on little land
Extensive — little labour on much land

blocks.text: Farming combines the factors of production in a season-specific way. Land provides the site, and its fertility, irrigation and size of holding decide what can be grown at all. Labour — human and, where affordable, animal or machine — performs sowing, weeding, spraying and harvesting, and its availability shapes whether the farm is labour-intensive or mechanised. Seeds determine yield potential before a single drop of water is applied; improved varieties can double output, which is why seed quality is a policy concern. Fertilisers and manure replace what each harvest removes from the soil, and irrigation supplies the water the monsoon promises but does not guarantee. Tools and machinery reduce drudgery and widen the area one family can cultivate, and credit pays for all of it between sowing and sale — the gap in which a farmer without financing must borrow at whatever terms are offered. Together these inputs turn a fixed natural resource into a recurring output, and the cost and reliability of each one shows up in the farm’s income.

items: Land: fertility, topography and holding size constrain what is possible before any effort is spent.
Seeds: the yield ceiling is set in the seed, which is why improved varieties spread so fast.
Irrigation: the difference between one assured crop and one gamble on the monsoon.
Fertilisers and manure: inputs that must replace what the harvest removes, or soil depletes.
Credit: finances inputs through the sowing-to-sale gap, at interest that directly reduces farm income.

learn.title: What farming produces, and for whom

blocks.text: The outputs of agriculture fall into three destinations. Food crops — cereals, pulses, oilseeds, sugar — feed the population directly and are therefore the backbone of food security: a shortfall in their harvest is felt first in prices and in the poorest households. Cash crops — cotton, jute, tea, coffee — supply industry with raw materials, which is how the primary sector feeds the secondary one. Livestock products — milk, eggs, wool, meat — add protein and, for small farmers, a steady income that does not wait for harvest season. The surplus of each output moves through the tertiary sector: mandis, storage, transport and trade carry it from field to consumer. How much of the output reaches the farmer rather than the intermediaries — the share of the consumer’s rupee that returns to the field — is the economic question behind every marketing reform.

items.meaning: Crops grown primarily to feed people: cereals, pulses, oilseeds and sugar crops.
items.context: Food crop output is the country’s food security in physical form.

items.meaning: Crops grown mainly for sale and for industry: cotton, jute, tea and coffee.
items.context: Cash crops convert a harvest into cash income and into industrial raw material.

items.meaning: A dependable physical supply of food for the population at affordable prices.
items.context: Food security depends on harvest levels, stocks, imports and distribution together.

items.meaning: Output beyond the producer’s own consumption, available for sale.
items.context: Only a surplus makes commercial farming and market supply possible.

learn.title: Agriculture’s place in the Indian economy

blocks.text: Agriculture’s role is larger than its income share suggests. It feeds the entire population, so its productivity sets the standard of living before anything else is considered: a good harvest lowers food prices for everyone, urban households included. It supplies the raw materials on which a large part of Indian industry stands — cotton for textiles, jute for packing, sugarcane for sugar, oilseeds for soap and cooking oil, and milk for a vast dairy industry. It is the source of livelihood for the majority of the workforce, which makes farm incomes the main engine of rural demand for industrial goods — clothing, utensils, bicycles, cement. And it earns export earnings through tea, spices, coffee and cotton products, bringing foreign exchange that pays for the imports industry needs. The paradox of the sector is that so much of the population depends on an activity whose share of national income has been shrinking — the productivity gap that the next lesson’s challenges describe.

items: Food supply: the entire population eats what farming produces, so its yield is a national welfare variable.
Industrial raw material: cotton, jute, sugar, oilseeds and milk feed secondary-sector production.
Employment: the majority of the workforce draws its livelihood from land-based activity.
Market demand: farm incomes are the base of rural consumption, which industry depends on.
Exports: tea, spices, coffee and cotton goods earn the foreign exchange that pays for imports.

learn.title: The pressures Indian agriculture works under

blocks.text: The challenges are structural rather than accidental. Holdings shrink with every division of inheritance, so much farming happens on plots too small for machinery or for risk-taking. Dependence on the monsoon remains high wherever irrigation has not reached, turning a large share of the crop into an annual wager. Input costs — seeds, fertiliser, fuel, credit — rise faster than the prices farmers receive, compressing margins into a thin band. Fragmented land makes investment uneconomic: few will build an irrigation channel that benefits four neighbours’ strips. And a farmer who must sell soon after harvest often meets the year’s lowest prices, while consumers meet the year’s highest later — a timing problem that storage and marketing reforms are designed to address. None of these is a reason farming fails; together they explain why it employs so much and earns so little, which is the central fact this chapter’s answers must handle.

items.text: Two brothers inherit a ten-acre farm; each son’s share divides again in the next generation.
items.note: Fragmentation: the holding shrinks by inheritance, not by any decision about efficiency.

items.text: A farmer without an irrigation pump depends entirely on the monsoon’s arrival date.
items.note: Monsoon dependence converts a single weather pattern into a household’s entire income risk.

learn.title: Government measures, the Green Revolution and food security

blocks.text: Farming’s problems drew a direct policy response, and the syllabus lists the measures as a connected package rather than as isolated schemes. High-yielding variety seeds raised the biological ceiling of each acre; chemical fertilisers and insecticides protected the added potential from nutrient loss and pest damage; better irrigation — tube wells, canals and tanks — watered the new varieties when the monsoon was late; improved farm technology and mechanisation cut the time between sowing and harvest; agricultural research centres and institutes generated and distributed the varieties, the practices and the extension advice that carried them to villages; rural credit facilities gave farmers an alternative to moneylenders so the package could actually be bought; and better storage and marketing arrangements kept the larger harvest from spoiling or being sold into a collapsing price. Each measure answers a specific failure identified earlier — seeds answer the yield ceiling, irrigation answers the monsoon gamble, credit answers the input gap — which is why the package worked better than any single measure would have.

The Green Revolution is the package’s most visible success: from the mid-1960s, high-yielding varieties of wheat and later rice, grown with irrigation and fertiliser, raised foodgrain output sharply within a few crop cycles. Its positive impacts are the syllabus’s focus — a large rise in production of foodgrains, movement towards self-sufficiency in food so that recurrent famine fears receded, a surplus available for buffer stocks and release schemes, growth of markets and of income in the adopting regions, and confidence that technology rather than rain alone could determine the harvest. Food security is the condition that follows: availability of food, its accessibility to people at affordable prices, and their ability to buy it at all times, not only in good years. The Food Corporation of India underpins all three — it procures grain at announced support prices from farmers, maintains buffer stocks against shortfall, and moves grain through the public distribution system so that prices stabilise and supplies reach deficit areas and vulnerable households. Procurement, storage and distribution are therefore one loop: the farmer gets a floor price that supports production, and the consumer gets a ceiling price that protects consumption — food security for both sides of the same market.

items.text: A wheat farmer in Punjab adopts HYV seed with assured canal water and fertiliser, and harvests several times the yield of an unirrigated plot of equal size.
items.note: The package working: seed potential, water and plant nutrition arrive together.

items.text: A failed monsoon year draws down FCI buffer stocks to keep ration prices stable in deficit states.
items.note: Food security in practice: procurement in good years buys stability in bad ones.

keyPoints: Agriculture is the cultivation of crops and rearing of animals — the primary sector’s largest activity in India.
Subsistence farming feeds the household first; commercial farming grows chiefly for sale.
Farming runs on land, labour, seeds, fertilisers, irrigation, tools and credit.
Improved seeds set a higher yield ceiling; irrigation removes the monsoon gamble.
Food crops feed the population; cash crops feed industry; livestock steadies farm income.
Agriculture supplies food security, industrial raw materials, employment, rural demand and exports.
Holdings fragment through inheritance, which blocks machinery and investment.
Input costs rising faster than farm prices is the margin squeeze behind the sector’s low income share.
Post-harvest selling into the year’s lowest prices is a timing problem storage and marketing can fix.
examFocus: Classify farming on the stated basis — purpose, intensity or organisation — and give a pair of examples.
List the inputs as a system, with one line on what each decides about the harvest.
Trace one cash crop into industry to show the primary–secondary link concretely.
Explain agriculture’s role through all five heads: food, materials, jobs, demand and exports.
Handle the employment-versus-income paradox explicitly: lots of people, small share of income, and why.
In challenge answers, pair each structural cause with its economic consequence.

vocabulary.context: Commercial farming converts the harvest into cash income and industrial supply.

vocabulary.meaning: A crop grown mainly for sale or for industry, such as cotton or jute.
vocabulary.context: Cash crops are how the primary sector feeds the secondary one.

vocabulary.context: Food security rests on harvest levels, buffer stocks and fair distribution.

vocabulary.context: Fragmentation blocks machinery, irrigation investment and risk-taking.

vocabulary.meaning: The artificial supply of water to crops, independent of the monsoon.
vocabulary.context: Irrigation converts a gamble on rain into a planned crop cycle.

questions.prompt: Subsistence farming differs from commercial farming because it:
options: Grows mainly to feed the farmer’s household
Never sells any output
Uses no bought inputs at all
Is always practised on large holdings
questions.answer: Grows mainly to feed the farmer’s household
questions.explanation: Purpose is the dividing line: subsistence farming feeds the family first and sells only surplus, while commercial farming grows chiefly for sale. Subsistence farms may still sell, buy inputs and be small — but the purpose is what defines them.
questions.commonMistake: Defining subsistence as farming that sells nothing — even a small farmer sells the surplus; the difference is priority.

questions.prompt: Which input sets the yield ceiling of a crop before water or fertiliser is applied?
options: The seed
The plough
The size of the barn
The market price
questions.explanation: The seed carries the variety’s genetic potential — how much it can yield under the best management. Tools, fertiliser and irrigation help the crop approach that potential, but they cannot exceed what the seed allows.
questions.commonMistake: Credit fertiliser with the highest yield effect — fertiliser closes the gap; the seed sets the ceiling.

questions.prompt: Cotton is classified as a cash crop because it is grown:
options: Mainly for sale and for industry
Only for the farmer’s own consumption
Without any purchased inputs
Exclusively on very large farms
questions.answer: Mainly for sale and for industry
questions.explanation: Cash crops are grown for the market: cotton supplies the textile industry and earns the farmer cash income. Food crops feed the household; cash crops feed industry and trade.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking cash crops are grown only for export — the defining feature is sale, not destination.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest reason small fragmented holdings resist mechanisation?
options: Machinery cannot be used economically on tiny scattered strips
Tractors are prohibited on small farms
Small farmers are uninterested in machines
Machinery works only in the tertiary sector
questions.answer: Machinery cannot be used economically on tiny scattered strips
questions.explanation: A machine’s cost is justified by the area it covers: on small scattered plots most of its time is spent moving between strips, and the per-acre cost defeats the saving. The economic obstacle is area, not interest or law.
questions.commonMistake: Blaming farmers’ attitudes — the constraint is structural: cost per acre on fragmented land.

questions.prompt: Complete: farming is broadly classified by purpose into ________ farming, which feeds the household, and ________ farming, which grows mainly for sale.
questions.explanation: Purpose is the primary classification: one looks inward to the household, the other outward to the market, and the other classifications — intensity and organisation — cut across both.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the pair, which would define commercial farming as feeding households.

questions.prompt: List four inputs of farming and state what each contributes.
questions.answer: Land provides the site and its fertility decides what can grow. Seeds set the yield potential of the crop before anything else is applied. Irrigation supplies water independently of the monsoon, turning a gamble into a plan. Credit finances the inputs through the gap between sowing and sale, so the farmer can buy seed and fertiliser without waiting for the harvest to pay. Fertilisers and manure replace what the harvest removes from the soil.
questions.explanation: Four inputs with one line each earn full marks; the strongest answers say what each input decides — site, ceiling, water security, and cash flow — rather than merely naming it.
questions.commonMistake: Listing inputs as words with no function, which shows vocabulary but not understanding of the farming system.

questions.prompt: State three roles agriculture plays in the Indian economy.
questions.answer: It ensures food security: the entire population eats what the land produces, so farm yield sets basic welfare and food prices for everyone. It supplies raw materials to industry: cotton for textiles, jute for packing, sugarcane for sugar and oilseeds for industry. It is the largest source of livelihood, employing the majority of the workforce, and its incomes form the base of rural demand for industrial goods. It also earns foreign exchange through exports of tea, spices, coffee and cotton products.
questions.explanation: Three roles with a mechanism each earn full marks; the fourth — exports — is the bonus. Linking farm incomes to rural demand shows the primary sector supporting the secondary one.
questions.commonMistake: Writing only that agriculture feeds people, missing its industrial, employment and trade roles entirely.

questions.prompt: Explain how a shortfall in the monsoon travels through the economy, using the interrelationship of sectors.
questions.answer: The chain begins in the primary sector: a weak monsoon means late or inadequate sowing, lower yields and a smaller harvest of food and cash crops alike. Food prices rise first — cereals and pulses are staples whose demand barely falls when prices climb, so the burden lands heaviest on low-income households, and food security itself becomes the question. The secondary sector feels it next in both directions: cotton, jute, oilseed and sugar processing run short of raw material, so mills work below capacity and workers are laid off, while higher food bills cut the rural incomes that bought cloth, utensils and cement — demand falls just as supply has tightened. The tertiary sector absorbs the shock through the same routes: transport carries fewer loads, mandis handle smaller arrivals, banks face loans that cannot be repaid from a failed crop, and the government spends on relief while collecting less agricultural tax revenue. Imports fill the gap if stocks are short, sending foreign exchange abroad instead of building reserves. The interrelationship explains the transmission: materials flow forward through the chain, incomes flow backward, and a monsoon failure interrupts both at once — which is why irrigation, buffer stocks and crop insurance exist, to break the link between one season’s weather and the whole economy’s working.
questions.explanation: The answer must walk the shock through all three sectors with concrete mechanisms — prices, capacity, demand, credit, revenue — and finish with the instruments that sever the transmission, since naming them shows why the interrelationship matters to policy.
questions.commonMistake: Stopping at “crops fail and prices rise”, which covers the primary sector only and never demonstrates interrelationship.

questions.prompt: “Indian agriculture employs the largest share of the workforce but produces a much smaller share of national income.” Explain this paradox and what it implies.
questions.answer: The paradox has one root: productivity per worker in agriculture is far below the economy-wide average. The majority of the workforce divides the sector’s output, so income per farm worker stays low, while industry and services generate more value with fewer people. Several structures produce that gap. Holdings fragment through inheritance until plots are too small to justify machinery, so much work is done by hand at low output per hour. Dependence on the monsoon persists wherever irrigation has not reached, making a share of every year’s output a wager rather than a plan. Input costs rise faster than the prices farmers receive, compressing the margin between them. And selling soon after harvest into the year’s lowest prices while consumers pay the year’s highest later drains value into intermediaries rather than to the field. The implications run through the whole economy: rural demand stays weak because farm incomes are low, which caps the market for industrial goods; migration to cities continues in search of the higher productivity the secondary and tertiary sectors offer; and public policy must raise farm productivity — irrigation, better seeds, credit, storage, marketing — rather than merely raise prices. The measure of success is output per worker, not output per acre alone, because the question is income for the people on the land.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the mechanism (output divided among too many workers), the structural causes listed with their economic logic, and the implications for demand, migration and policy. Ending on output per worker as the correct metric makes the answer analytical.
questions.commonMistake: Repeating the statistics without mechanism, or concluding that agriculture is unimportant — its employment share is exactly why its productivity matters.

questions.prompt: A farmer must choose between selling the harvest immediately or storing it for four months. Analyse the choice using inputs, market timing and opportunity cost.
questions.answer: The two paths differ on price, cost and risk, and each has a real opportunity cost. Selling immediately converts the crop into cash at the year’s lowest price — the glut right after harvest is when arrivals are heaviest — but the cost is near zero and the cash can repay the input credit that is already accruing interest. Storing aims at the higher price of the lean season, but it carries costs that must be counted as part of the choice: warehouse charges, interest that keeps running on the borrowed input money, physical loss to moisture and pests, and the risk that the price rise expected does not come. The opportunity cost of selling now is the price difference the storage might have earned, net of those costs; the opportunity cost of storing is the cash that could have cleared debt, bought the next season’s inputs at an earlier discount, or fed the household in the months before the new harvest. The decision therefore turns on whether the expected price gain exceeds storage cost plus interest plus risk — for a farmer with cheap storage and no urgent debt, storage can win; for one carrying high-interest loans, selling into the post-harvest glut may be the cheaper sacrifice. This is why storage capacity and institutional credit change farmer behaviour: each removes one of the costs that forces a distress sale.
questions.explanation: The analysis must price all three elements — the price-timing gain, the full cost of holding, and each side’s opportunity cost — and reach a conditional conclusion tied to the farmer’s debt and storage position, which is what shows the concept working rather than being defined.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming storage is always better because prices rise later, ignoring interest and storage costs that can exceed the price gain.

questions.prompt: The Food Corporation of India contributes to food security primarily by:
options: Procuring grain at support prices, holding buffer stocks and distributing through the public distribution system
Manufacturing fertiliser for farmers
Setting the interest rate on rural credit
Certifying organic farm exports
questions.answer: Procuring grain at support prices, holding buffer stocks and distributing through the public distribution system
questions.explanation: FCI underpins all three faces of food security — availability, accessibility and affordability — by buying grain from farmers, storing buffer stocks against shortfall, and moving supplies to deficit areas and vulnerable households at stable prices.
questions.commonMistake: Assigning FCI input supply functions: seeds, fertiliser and credit are agricultural support measures, while FCI handles the grain itself.

questions.prompt: State four measures taken by the government to increase agricultural production.
questions.answer: High-yielding variety seeds were distributed to raise the output potential of each acre. Fertilisers and insectisers replaced the soil nutrients each harvest removed and protected the crop from pests. Better irrigation — tube wells, canals and tanks — watered the crop independently of the monsoon’s timing. Agricultural research centres and institutes generated improved varieties and practices and carried them to farmers through extension advice. Rural credit facilities let farmers buy this package without moneylenders, and improved storage and marketing kept the larger harvest from spoiling or being sold into a collapsing price.
questions.explanation: Four measures with one line of purpose each earn full marks; the strongest answers connect each measure to the constraint it removes — yield ceiling, crop loss, water timing, credit gap, post-harvest loss.
questions.commonMistake: Listing measure names with no purpose, or naming the Green Revolution itself as a measure instead of as the result of the measures combined.
